title: Réti's manoeuvre
summary: King and pawn against king and pawn: the king that chases two hares and saves what looked lost.
part.reti.title: Réti's position
part.reti.summary: The king outside the square and the pawn about to be stopped: the diagonal that draws.
part.push.title: If the pawn runs
part.push.summary: When Black runs with the pawn, the white king goes to support its own.
part.marshall.title: The manoeuvre for Black
part.marshall.summary: Yates against Marshall, Karlsbad 1929: the same idea with the colours reversed, in a real game.
part.piece.title: A piece in the way
part.piece.summary: When a bishop guards the queening square, the first step of the diagonal attacks it and gains the missing tempo.
part.limits.title: When the manoeuvre comes too late
part.limits.summary: One more step of the pawn and the diagonal does not make it: count the tempi before trusting it.
part.recap.title: Summary
part.recap.summary: Checking whether the pawn queens on its own, three rules to take with you and an ending to play.
step.t_reti: The white king is far from the h5-pawn, and the black king catches the c6-pawn easily. It looks lost. Is there a path for the white king that saves the game? What is the first move?
step.t_reti.hint1: Chasing the h5-pawn down the h-file is too slow. But the king does not have to walk in a straight line.
step.t_reti.hint2: Look for a square that brings the king closer to the h5-pawn and, at the same time, closer to its own pawn.
step.intro: The answer is 1.Kg7! Before seeing why, see why it looks lost. Richard Réti published this position in 1921, and it still fools masters. The square of the h5-pawn runs from d5 to h1, and my king is not inside it: in a plain race, the pawn queens. And my c6-pawn? The black king reaches b7 in one move and stops it. Two lost causes, it seems.
step.diagonal: Now the secret, which is pure geometry. From h8 to h4, down the file, is four moves. To f4, along the diagonal 1.Kg7, 2.Kf6, 3.Ke5 and 4.Kf4, is also four, and f4 is inside the pawn's square. On a chessboard, the king that zigzags loses no time at all. And from e5 the king threatens two things: stepping into the square of the black pawn, and reaching d6 to support the white pawn. Gurvich called it hunting two hares at once.
step.d_main: I will play the main line for both sides. Notice how Black, on every move, has to choose which threat to meet.
step.d_main.m1: 1.Kg7! The only move. The king starts down the diagonal and is already closer to both pawns.
step.d_main.m2: 1...h4. Black runs with the pawn. It is still far from queening.
step.d_main.m3: 2.Kf6. Now the threat is 3.Ke5, stepping into the square and heading for d6 at the same time.
step.d_main.m4: 2...Kb6. The black king goes for the c6-pawn. If it runs with the pawn, my king supports mine, as you will see in the next part.
step.d_main.m5: 3.Ke5! This is the point. If Black pushes the pawn, I go to d6 and my pawn queens too. So Black has to spend a tempo taking the c6-pawn.
step.d_main.m6: 3...Kxc6. Black captures the pawn. That was the tempo I needed.
step.d_main.m7: 4.Kf4. My king has stepped into the square of the h4-pawn, and the rest is counting: 4...h3 5.Kg3 h2 6.Kxh2, a draw. A king that seemed far from everything arrived in time on both sides of the board.
step.main: Your turn, with White. This time the black king goes after your pawn first. Find the diagonal and draw.
step.main.hint: The road is the same: 1.Kg7, 2.Kf6 and 3.Ke5. Every move has to threaten both things at once. Once the c6-pawn falls, step into the square of the black pawn.
step.main.done: Well done. Black changed the move order, but the diagonal was the same. 4.Ke4 was also fine on the last move.
step.t_push: Black did not waste time on your pawn: while the white king went from h8 to f6, Black ran with its own, which is already on h3. It queens before your king gets there. What is left for White?
step.t_push.hint1: If you cannot stop the black pawn, maybe you can queen as well. Where does your king need to be for that?
step.push: Here the second hare shows up. The black pawn can no longer be caught. But Black spent its moves on the pawn, not on the king, and my king on f6 is close to d7. That is why 1.Ke7! If the king reaches d7, my pawn queens together with Black's.
step.d_push: Watch the two queens appear almost together.
step.d_push.m1: 1.Ke7. The king goes near d7 and d8, the squares that guard the queening square. 1.Ke6 was also fine.
step.d_push.m2: 1...h2. The black pawn reaches the second rank.
step.d_push.m3: 2.c7. My pawn advances, and the king already covers d8.
step.d_push.m4: 2...Kb7. The black king tries to stop the pawn from the front.
step.d_push.m5: 3.Kd7. The king covers c8: the black king on b7 will not be able to capture the queen that is about to appear.
step.d_push.m6: 3...h1=Q. Black queens first, but the new queen neither gives check nor attacks c8.
step.d_push.m7: 4.c8=Q+. My pawn also becomes a queen, with check. Queen against queen and nothing else on the board: a draw.
step.late: And if Black runs only later, when my king is already on e5? On e5 the king was ready for both jobs. The black pawn has escaped the square, so the king goes next to the c6-pawn, and my pawn queens in time. The same idea, one move later.
step.lateMove: White to play and draw. The black pawn has just advanced to h3.
step.lateMove.hint: The black pawn can no longer be caught. Bring the king next to your pawn and prepare to queen.
step.lateMove.done: That's it. 1.Kd6, 2.c7 and 3.Kd7: both queens appear, and the ending is a draw.
step.t_marshall: Now you are Black, in a real game. The a4-pawn is going to fall, and the white f2-pawn is far from your king. How does Black save the game?
step.t_marshall.hint1: Remember Réti: the king does not have to walk in a straight line to reach the f2-pawn.
step.t_marshall.hint2: Look for a square that threatens to support the a4-pawn's advance and, at the same time, brings the king closer to the white pawn.
step.marshall: Yates against Marshall, Karlsbad 1929, round 9. There had been a race: White queened first but could not stop Black's b2-pawn, and Yates traded queens with 58.Kc4 b1=Q 59.Qxb1+ Kxb1 60.Kb4. The pawn ending looked won: the a4-pawn falls and the f2-pawn is far from the black king. Marshall saw the diagonal and played 60...Kb2! The king threatens to support 61...a3, which White could no longer capture, and at the same time heads for f2.
step.d_marshall: Watch the end of the game, move by move.
step.d_marshall.m1: 60...Kb2! The king threatens 61...a3 with the pawn supported, and takes the first step along the diagonal b2, c3, d4.
step.d_marshall.m2: 61.Kxa4. Yates captures the pawn, but spends on it the move he needed to run with the f2-pawn.
step.d_marshall.m3: 61...Kc3! The king steps into the square of the f2-pawn: if it runs, the king catches it.
step.d_marshall.m4: 62.f4. The pawn runs, but the king is already close.
step.d_marshall.m5: 62...Kd4. The king is one step from the pawn: if 63.f5, then 63...Ke5 and 64...Kxf6 after 64.f6. The game was drawn here.
step.wrong: The natural mistake was 60...Kc2? The king heads straight for the centre, but it neither protects the a4-pawn nor threatens anything. White would play 61.f4! The pawn runs: 61...Kd3 62.f5 Ke4 63.f6 Ke5 64.f7, and it queens. One different move, a different result.
step.marshallMove: Black to play and draw. Do what Marshall did.
step.marshallMove.hint: The first move has to do two jobs: look after the a4-pawn and bring the king closer to the f2-pawn.
step.marshallMove.done: Perfect. 60...Kb2, 61...Kc3 and 62...Kd4: the black king steps into the pawn's square and the draw is safe. 62...Kc4 was also fine at the end.
step.t_piece: Now there is a bishop on the board. The f6-bishop guards d8, so the d7-pawn cannot queen. The b4-pawn runs to b1, and the white king on g4 is outside its square. How does White draw?
step.t_piece.hint1: Counting is not enough: on the direct road the king arrives one move late. It has to gain a tempo.
step.t_piece.hint2: The bishop has a job: guarding d8. What happens if it is attacked?
step.piece: 1.Kf5! The direct road, 1.Kf3? b3 2.Ke2 b2 3.Kd2 b1=Q, arrives one move late. The diagonal through f5, e4 and d3 to c2 is just as long, but its first step attacks the bishop. The move the bishop spends escaping is the tempo I was missing. With a piece in the way, the right diagonal is the one that attacks it. And check the road before you walk: sometimes what blocks a diagonal is one of your own pawns, which lands on it after an exchange. Look at your opponent's pawn breaks before you choose.
step.d_piece: Watch the king gain the missing tempo.
step.d_piece.m1: 1.Kf5! It attacks the bishop and takes the first step towards c2.
step.d_piece.m2: 1...Be7. The bishop escapes and keeps guarding d8 (1...Bd8 and 1...Bh4 are the same), but the b4-pawn stood still. If 1...b3, 2.Kxf6 b2 3.d8=Q b1=Q and there are two queens: a draw.
step.d_piece.m3: 2.Ke4. The king follows the diagonal; now it is two steps from c2.
step.d_piece.m4: 2...b3. Now the pawn runs, one move late.
step.d_piece.m5: 3.Kd3. One more step: next move the king reaches c2.
step.d_piece.m7: 4.Kc2. The king covers b1: the pawn falls, and the bishop alone cannot win. A draw.
step.pieceMove: White to play and draw. Another piece in the way: the e6-bishop guards c8, and the a4-pawn runs to a1.
step.pieceMove.hint: Look for the diagonal whose first step attacks the bishop and whose next steps bring the king into the square of the a4-pawn.
step.pieceMove.done: That's it. 1.Ke5! and then 2.Kd4, 3.Kc3 and 4.Kb2: the bishop had to spend a move, and the king arrived in time.
step.t_far: Now you play Black. It is Réti's position, but the black pawn started on h4, one step further, and the white king has already gone to g7. Does the manoeuvre still save White, or does Black win?
step.t_far.hint1: Count the white king's moves to the pawn's square and to d7, and compare them with the pawn's moves to h1.
step.far: Black wins, and the move is 1...h3. The diagonal is as fast as before, but the pawn is one step closer to queening. The white king arrives late in both places: when it threatens to enter the square, the pawn has already left it; when it goes to support its own pawn, Black's queen is born first. Réti's manoeuvre is a calculation, and a calculation can come out wrong.
step.d_far: Watch the same diagonal arrive one move late.
step.d_far.m1: 1...h3. The pawn is already two steps from queening.
step.d_far.m2: 2.Kf6. Réti's diagonal, just as in the original position.
step.d_far.m3: 2...Kb6. The black king calmly goes for the c6-pawn: Black has a tempo to spare.
step.d_far.m4: 3.Ke5. The square of the two threats, but now neither arrives in time.
step.d_far.m5: 3...h2. The pawn gets away: the white king can no longer enter the square.
step.d_far.m6: 4.Kd6. The king rushes to support the c6-pawn, too late.
step.d_far.m7: 4...h1=Q. The queen is born while the white pawn is still on c6: Black wins.
step.farMove: Black to play and win. Now it is your turn to show that White's diagonal comes too late.
step.farMove.hint: The black king does not need to chase the c6-pawn. Count: your pawn runs faster than the white king.
step.farMove.done: That's it. The pawn queens before anything else happens. 1...Kb6 also won: the spare tempo belongs to Black.
step.front: Now the limit seen from the other side. Black to play and win, but the white pawn is on d6, one step closer to queening. If the black king goes to capture it with 1...Kc6?, 2.Kf5! is Réti's diagonal again, and the tempo spent on the capture saves White. The right move is 1...Kc8! The black king neither captures nor runs: it stops the pawn from the front. With the white pawn blocked, neither threat exists any more, and the h4-pawn queens at leisure.
step.frontMove: Black to play and win. Stop the white pawn before thinking about yours.
step.frontMove.hint: Neither run with the pawn nor go and capture the d6-pawn: look for the square from which the black king gets in front of the white pawn.
step.frontMove.done: That's it. 1...Kc8! and 2...Kd7: the king is in front of the pawn, and the white king has nothing left to threaten. 2...Kd8 was also fine.
step.t_close: It is almost Réti's position, but the black king is on a5, one square further from the c6-pawn. Before looking for the diagonal, ask the question: does White need the manoeuvre at all?
step.t_close.hint1: Count your pawn's moves to c8 and the black king's moves to c7.
step.close: No, it does not. 1.c7! The black king on a5 reaches b6 in one move, but not c7, and the pawn queens first. Here the manoeuvre, 1.Kg7, would only draw. It is the first check in any ending like this: does my pawn queen on its own?
step.rules: Three rules. First: count before anything else; if your pawn queens on its own, you need no manoeuvre, and one more step of the enemy pawn ruins the manoeuvre; and, against it, a king that stops the pawn from the front is worth more than one that rushes to capture it. Second: on the diagonal the king moves as fast as in a straight line, and it sees more of the board. Third: look for the square that threatens two things, because your opponent can only meet one; with a piece in the way, the right diagonal is the one that attacks it.
step.mirrorMove: The idea does not care which side of the board it is on. Here is Réti's position in the mirror: king on a8, white pawn on f6, black pawn on a5. White to play and draw.
step.mirrorMove.hint: Walk along the diagonal towards the centre: every move brings the king closer to both pawns.
step.mirrorMove.done: Well done. 1.Kb7, 2.Kc6, 3.Kd5 and 4.Kc4: the same manoeuvre on the other side. 4.Kd4 was also fine at the end.
step.finish: Now play it to the end. The king starts on g8 instead of h8, and your opponent defends Black as well as it can. Find the diagonal and hold the draw.
ex.e08: The white king has already gone to g7, but the black king is on a7. Find the winning move.
ex.e08.hint: Pawn first. Then, when the white king threatens to support the c6-pawn, put your king in front of it.
ex.e08.solution: 1...h4 (1...Kb8 too) and, after 2.Kf6, 2...Kb8! The black king stands in front of the c6-pawn before the white king arrives to support it, and the h4-pawn keeps running. With the black king on a7, Réti's manoeuvre comes too late.
ex.e09: Réti, 1928. White to play and draw. Now there are more black pawns.
ex.e09.hint: The king eats pawns along the way, but always on the diagonal that leads to its own pawn.
ex.e09.solution: 1.Kg6!, then 2.Kxg7 and 3.Kxf6. The king takes two pawns without leaving the diagonal that leads to e5 and d6, and Réti's idea does the rest.
ex.e10: Lasker against Tarrasch, 1914, after 41...Kxh4. White to play and draw.
ex.e10.hint: The king has to go back to the queenside pawns, and there are two routes of the same length. Before you choose, look at the break 42...c4: after the exchanges, a white pawn can end up in your king's path.
ex.e10.solution: 42.Kf5! The natural 42.Kf6? loses to 42...c4! 43.bxc4 bxc4 44.Ke5 c3! 45.bxc3 a4: the white pawn on c3 stands on the square the king needed, and after 46.Kd4 a3 47.Kc4 a2 Black's pawn queens. Along the f5 diagonal the king reaches d3 in time: 42...c4 43.bxc4 bxc4 44.Ke4 c3 45.Kd3 cxb2 46.Kc2, and it catches Black's pawns. In the game Tarrasch played 42...Kg3, and after 43.Ke4 Kf2 44.Kd5 Lasker's king captured all three queenside pawns: a draw. The theme came back later in Réti's study.
ex.e11: Sarychev's study. White to play and draw. Careful: queening right away loses the queen.
ex.e11.hint: If the pawn queens now, the bishop checks and wins the queen. Start with a king move that protects the pawn and attacks something.
ex.e11.solution: 1.Kc8!! The king stays glued to the pawn and attacks the b7-pawn. After 1...b5 it comes back along the diagonal: 2.Kd7, 3.Kd6 and 4.Ke5, which attacks the bishop; on the next move, 5.Kd4 catches the pawn. It is Réti with a bishop in the way.
ex.e12: Prokeš study. White to play and draw. The black king stands between your king and the h7-pawn.
ex.e12.hint: The direct road to the h7-pawn is shut. Look for a route on which every king move threatens to support the a5-pawn, so Black has no time to run with theirs.
ex.e12.solution: 1.Kc8!, 2.Kb8! and 3.Kb7! The king moves away from the h7-pawn, but every move threatens to support the a5-pawn, and if Black runs with 3...h5, 4.a6 queens. Black has to spend time taking the a5-pawn; after 3...Kxa5, 4.Kc6 and 5.Kd5 step into the square of the pawn. 1.a6? and 1.Ke8? lose.
ex.e13: A study attributed to Réti. White to play and draw. The black bishop watches the queening square, and the g6-pawn is about to run.
ex.e13.hint: Pushing the pawn now lets the bishop hold it from afar. King first. Then look for a way back on which the king attacks the bishop and approaches the black pawn at the same time.
ex.e13.solution: 1.Ke7! (1.e7? Bb5 and the bishop holds e8 on its own) 1...g5, 2.Kd6 g4, 3.e7 Bb5 and now 4.Kc5!, attacking the bishop. The bishop must keep watching e8 and cannot use the other diagonal, which its own g4-pawn closes. The king walks back down the diagonal: 5.Kd4, 6.Ke3 and 7.Kf2, and catches the pawn. Every move is the only one.
ex.e14: A study attributed to Réti. White to play and draw. The black king threatens to take the d5-pawn and then the g4-pawn.
ex.e14.hint: Use the d5-pawn to lure the black king away from the kingside. After that, your king needs a waiting move to put Black in zugzwang.
ex.e14.solution: 1.d6! Ke6 2.d7! Kxd7 and 3.Ka7! After 3...Bc8, 4.Kb8! puts Black in zugzwang, because the bishop has to stay on c8 or on the a6–c8 diagonal. After 4...Ba6, 5.Ka7 again; 5...Kxc7 6.Kxa6 and the king comes back along the diagonal: 7.Kb5, 8.Kc4 and 9.Kd3, in time to reach f1 against the h6-pawn. 1.Kb8? and 1.Ka7? on the first move lose.
key.reti: The white king seems far from everything: it cannot catch the black pawn or help its own. But walking along the diagonal it chases both at once, and White draws.
key.yatesMarshall: Yates against Marshall, Karlsbad 1929: Marshall used the same idea with Black. His king walked diagonally, threatening both to support its own pawn and to hunt the white one, and saved the draw.
history: This is one of the most famous studies in chess history. In 1921 the Czech master Richard Réti published a position with just four pieces, in which a king that seems hopelessly far away saves the game. The secret is to walk diagonally: on a chessboard, a diagonal route takes as many moves as a straight one, and each step serves two plans at once. The composer Abram Gurvich called the idea the hunt of two hares. It had already appeared in a real game: in 1914, in St Petersburg, Lasker saved a pawn ending against Tarrasch that looked lost. And in 1929, in Karlsbad, Marshall used the same manoeuvre against Yates and drew.
practice: Now Réti's position for real, in the practical challenge. Find the diagonal and hold the draw. Pick your pace and go.
